newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - Polish central bank picks money mkt dealers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Polish central bank picks money mkt dealers.

text.p: The Polish central bank awarded 17 banks money market dealer status for 1997, entitling them to participate in its open market operations, the National Bank of Poland (NBP) said in a statement on Thursday.
Money market dealers, appointed annually, will be allowed to participate in the NBP's repos and reverse repos, in primary NBP-bill outrights and also gain greater profile.
Currently, 29 banks can take part in the central bank's operations under individual agreements signed with the NBP.

Earlier this year, 40 commercial banks interested in winning the status began competing for points on the so-called "dealers' activity index" (IAD). Banks must collect at least 46 of a maximum 80 IAD points in the June-November reviewing period to win the status.
Points were awarded for treasury bill sales to non-banking domestic investors; for share of the secondary T-bill market and NBP-bill trading and for quality of service.
Banks seeking money market dealer status in 1998 will be evaluated in April-November 1997.

Turnover on the secondary T-bill market almost doubled to 51.8 billion zlotys since the evaluation period started in July and trade in NBP-bills rocketed to 17 billion zlotys in November from July's 512 million. The average daily portfolio of T-bills in the domestic non-banking sector rose to nine billion zlotys last month from 6.37 billion in July.
The purpose of the new money market system, which comes into force next year, is to increase the scope for financing the budget deficit in the domestic non-financial sector.

"Money supply would have been bigger in 1996 if there had been no non-inflationary financing of the deficit by the non- banking sector," said Jacek Osinski, deputy head of the NBP's monetary policy department.

Osinski said the significant rise in non-banking T-bill portfolios prevented price swings on the local market when foreign investors were cutting their Polish T-bill portfolios in the second quarter of 1996.
"Foreigners withdrew three billion zlotys from Polish T-bills without any major price swings, because the same amount had been bought by non-banking customers," Osinski said.
But bankers noted that the new system also led to the shift of corporates from banking deposits to high-yielding T-bills.
